# Grouped bar graphs {#sec-grp-bar-graphs} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"} ## Theme: `theme_jurassic()` Graphs in this chapter use `ggrewindr::theme_jurassic()`, modeled on the Jurassic Park (1993) Post Office souvenir stamp sheet: a black sheet with a logo red frame, a dark jungle plot area, stamp yellow titles, red, yellow, sunset orange, cream, and tan marks, and a Herculanum title. ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false} ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a categorical variable** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a numeric (continuous) variable** :::
::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](grp_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: :::: ## Description Grouped bar graphs compare multiple values across categories. Each category has a cluster of bars. X-axis labels show categories and y-axis values. Colors or patterns differentiate subsets, and a legend is shown on the side or top of the graph. `geom_col()` displays 'grouped' numbers across the levels (or groups) of a categorical variable. ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Install packages. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation library(tidyr) # for uncount() ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: In [*Jurassic Park* (1993)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0107290/), every species lives in its own paddock. We'll simulate the weight of every dinosaur on two islands: Isla Nublar (the park) and Isla Sorna (Site B from [*The Lost World* (1997)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0119567/)). Both islands have the same five species, and each species gets a head count on each island (`n`) and its own normal distribution of weights (`mean_tons` and `sd_tons`). `tidyr::uncount()` repeats each row `n` times (one row per dinosaur), and `rnorm()` draws each dinosaur's weight. Then we add up the weights in each paddock on each island (`total_tons`). Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same dinosaurs every time you run the code below. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} set.seed(1993) # same dinosaur weights every time the code runs jp_dinos <- tibble( island = rep(c("Isla Nublar", "Isla Sorna"), each = 5), # the park and the second island species = rep(c("Brachiosaurus", "Triceratops", "Tyrannosaurus", # five species on each island "Gallimimus", "Velociraptor"), times = 2), n = c(3, 5, 2, 20, 8, # number of animals of each species on Isla Nublar 2, 7, 3, 14, 12), # number of animals of each species on Isla Sorna mean_tons = rep(c(40, 9, 8, 0.45, 0.15), times = 2), # average weight (tons), same on both islands sd_tons = rep(c(5, 1.2, 1, 0.08, 0.03), times = 2) # spread of each species' weights ) |> tidyr::uncount(n) |> # one row per animal mutate( weight_tons = round(rnorm(n(), mean = mean_tons, sd = sd_tons), 2) # each animal's weight ) |> select(island, species, weight_tons) jp_paddocks <- jp_dinos |> group_by(island, species) |> # one group per paddock on each island summarise(total_tons = sum(weight_tons), .groups = "drop") # total weight in each paddock glimpse(jp_paddocks) #> Rows: 10 #> Columns: 3 #> $ island "Isla Nublar", "Isla Nublar",… #> $ species "Brachiosaurus", "Gallimimus"… #> $ total_tons 115.83, 8.88, 43.08, 15.27, 1… ``` ::: ::: ## Distribution A grouped bar graph shows one number per group, and here that number is a total. Totals depend on two things: how many dinosaurs live in a paddock and how much each one weighs. Twenty Gallimimus still weigh less than two Tyrannosaurs. Below we'll move from the dinosaurs, to a picture, to the formula. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first six dinosaurs. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} head(jp_dinos, 6) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: Each Brachiosaurus weighs close to 40 tons, and each Triceratops weighs close to 9. For every paddock, the total is the number of dinosaurs times their average weight. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} jp_dinos |> group_by(island, species) |> summarise( dinosaurs = n(), mean_tons = mean(weight_tons), total_tons = sum(weight_tons)) #> `summarise()` has regrouped the output. #> ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by island and #> species. #> ℹ Output is grouped by island. #> ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to #> silence this message. #> ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(island, species))` for #> per-operation grouping (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) #> instead. ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: Each bar in a grouped bar graph is a bar model: a total made of parts. Below we draw every dinosaur on Isla Nublar as its own segment and stack the segments in each paddock. The height of each stack is the paddock's total, and the number of segments is its head count. The Gallimimus bar has 20 thin segments, and the Brachiosaurus bar has three thick ones. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} jp_dinos |> filter(island == "Isla Nublar") |> ggplot(aes(x = species, y = weight_tons, fill = species)) + geom_col(color = "#111111", linewidth = 0.3, show.legend = FALSE) + scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2)) + labs(x = "Paddock", y = "Total weight (tons)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](grp_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/draw_grp_col-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: Each dinosaur's weight comes from a [normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution) for its species, $X_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu, \sigma)$. A paddock's total adds up $n$ of these weights: $$ T = X_1 + X_2 + \dots + X_n \sim \text{Normal}(n\mu, \; \sqrt{n}\,\sigma) $$ The expected total is $n\mu$: $3 \times 40 = 120$ tons for the Brachiosaurus paddock and $20 \times 0.45 = 9$ tons for Gallimimus. The spread grows with $\sqrt{n}$, not $n$, because heavy and light dinosaurs partly cancel each other out. Our Brachiosaurus paddock on Isla Nublar weighs 115.8 tons, within one standard deviation ($\sqrt{3} \times 5 \approx 8.7$ tons) of its expected 120. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CHANGE IT:** ::: So far the graph shows what we expect: the heavy species have the tallest bars on both islands. Now we'll change the head counts of each dinosaur. Isla Sorna has no fences, and in the 1997 sequel its dinosaurs have been breeding on their own for years. Suppose the Gallimimus herd there grew from 14 to 300. We still expect each Gallimimus to weigh under half a ton, so the herd's bar should grow, but how much? ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} set.seed(1993) # same seed as above jp_herd <- jp_dinos |> bind_rows(tibble( island = "Isla Sorna", species = "Gallimimus", weight_tons = round(rnorm(286, mean = 0.45, sd = 0.08), 2))) # 286 more Gallimimus jp_paddocks_herd <- jp_herd |> group_by(island, species) |> summarise(dinosaurs = n(), total_tons = sum(weight_tons), .groups = "drop") jp_paddocks_herd ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: Below we redraw the same grouped bar graph with the new totals. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} ggplot(data = jp_paddocks_herd, aes(x = species, y = total_tons)) + geom_col(aes(fill = island), position = "dodge") + scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2)) + labs(x = "Paddock", y = "Total weight (tons)", fill = "Island") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](grp_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/change_graph_grp_col-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: The lightest species now has the tallest bar in the graph. The Isla Sorna Gallimimus weigh 133.8 tons together, more than the 115.8 tons of Brachiosaurus on Isla Nublar. Nothing about a single Gallimimus changed; only the head count did. The bar can't tell us whether its height comes from a few heavy animals or hundreds of light ones. I've found it's worth checking the counts (like the `dinosaurs` column above) before reading a tall bar of totals as a sign of big animals. ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: Grouped bar graphs expect the bar heights to already sit in a variable. We map that variable to the `x` or `y` aesthetic. - Create labels with `labs()` - Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data` - Map `species` to the `x` and `total_tons` to the `y` - Map `island` to `fill` *inside* the `aes()` of `geom_col()` - Place each island's bars side by side with `position = "dodge"` - Stagger the long paddock names over two lines with `scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2))` ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_grp_col <- labs( title = "Jurassic Park", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Total weight of the dinosaurs in each paddock, by island", x = "Paddock", y = "Total weight (tons)", fill = "Island") ggp2_grp_col <- ggplot(data = jp_paddocks, aes(x = species, y = total_tons)) + geom_col(aes(fill = island), position = "dodge") + scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2)) ggp2_grp_col + labs_grp_col ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](grp_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/create_graph_grp_col-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ## More info We didn't have to calculate `total_tons` (displayed on the `y` axis) by `species` because `ggplot2` does this for us! If we pass a categorical variable to the `x` (like `species`) and a continuous variable to `y` (like `weight_tons`), `stat_summary()` with `fun = "sum"` adds up `y` for each level of `x` and each `island`. `geom_col()` can't do this with `position = "dodge"`, because it draws each dinosaur's bar on top of the others instead of adding them up: ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jp_dinos |> ggplot(aes(x = species, y = weight_tons)) + stat_summary(aes(fill = island), fun = "sum", geom = "col", position = "dodge") + scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2)) + labs_grp_col ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](grp_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/create_summary_sum_col_graph-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: We can see the underlying totals using `dplyr`'s `group_by()` and `summarise()` functions. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jp_dinos |> dplyr::group_by(island, species) |> dplyr::summarise( `Total weight (tons)` = sum(weight_tons) ) |> dplyr::ungroup() |> dplyr::select(Island = island, `Paddock` = species, `Total weight (tons)`) ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Island Paddock Total weight (tons)
Isla Nublar Brachiosaurus 115.83
Isla Nublar Gallimimus 8.88
Isla Nublar Triceratops 43.08
Isla Nublar Tyrannosaurus 15.27
Isla Nublar Velociraptor 1.33
Isla Sorna Brachiosaurus 84.18
Isla Sorna Gallimimus 6.16
Isla Sorna Triceratops 63.48
Isla Sorna Tyrannosaurus 22.84
Isla Sorna Velociraptor 1.76
````` ::: ::: :::
